It started with the email.Came through just before dawn, when the office was at its worst, flickerring lights, stale air, that
half-drunk tea someone had abandoned days ago now wearing a skin.

Meeting — 9:00 Friday.
He’d done forty nights straight by then.
Forty.
Not that anyone was counting.
You just carry on, like something nailed in place.
They were already gathered when he got there.
Dave by the wall, arms folded.
Meena sat down, coat still on like she didn’t intend to stay.
Three of them.
Across the table, HR.
Another man beside them, quiet, watching.
It had the feel of something arranged in advance.
Not a meeting. More like a verdict waiting to be read out.
They spoke gently.
“Restructuring.”

“Unfortunately.”
“Nothing to do with performance.”
He noticed they never said his name once.
Three chairs opposite. Three decisions made somewhere else.
They went through it one by one, like a script.
Pause. Nod. Slide of paper across the table.
He didn’t argue.
Didn’t even ask much.
What would be the point? You don’t win those rooms.
At the end, they stood.
So he stood.
They shook hands.
That was the bit that stuck with him, the handshakes. Firm. Professional. Like they were thanking
him for something.

Like he was leaving on good terms.
Outside, the air hit him sharp.
Morning had broken properly now. Pale sun over the car park. Daffodils out along the edge like they’d
heard different news entirely.

Dave lit a cigarette.
“Bit of a stitch-up,” he said.
He nodded.
Didn’t say anything else.
Didn’t trust himself to.
He carried it home with him.
Didn’t open the envelope.
Just put it on the kitchen side like something you don’t want to look at directly.
His wife glanced at it, then at him.

“Alright?” she said.
“Yeah,” he said.
That was all they managed.
Saturday, he disappeared.
Not dramatically. No slammed doors, no words. Just went upstairs mid-morning and lay down.
Curtains drawn.
Light cut off.
The room held him there.
Not sleep exactly.
The kind of stillness where even time seems to hesitate.
Downstairs, life carried on.
The kids.
The kettle.
A radio voice drifting in and out.
His wife came in once, left a cup of tea on the bedside table. Didn’t wake him. Didn’t try.
By afternoon the tea had gone cold.
By evening the room had gone dark again.
He hadn’t moved much at all.
Sunday morning came quietly.
Light first. Thin at the edges of the curtain.
Then sound — foil tearing, small voices rising and falling.
He opened his eyes.
Lay there a moment, not quite sure what had shifted.
Nothing had, really.
And yet.
Downstairs, the kitchen was already alive.

Chocolate eggs spread across the table. Bright wrappers catching the light. The kids halfway through
them before breakfast like it was allowed just this once.

His wife stood at the counter, sleeves rolled, already in motion.
“Morning,” she said.
Like it was any other day.
He kissed her cheek. She leaned into it, just for a second.
The kettle clicked.
They cracked the eggs open properly then.
Foil peeled back. Hollow shells split.
Little plastic toys scattered across the table.
Arguments about size. About fairness.
He found himself smiling at it.
Didn’t plan to. Just happened.
By midday the house smelled of lamb.
Proper roast. The kind you only do when it’s meant to matter. Potatoes crisped right, soft in the
middle. Windows open a touch to let the heat out, though it never quite did.

He carved, same as always.
Knife steady in his hand.
“Bit more?” he said.
They all said no.
Then took more anyway.
Nothing had changed.
The envelope was still there on the side.
Monday was still coming.
The job still gone.
But the table was full.
His kids loud and sticky with chocolate.

His wife moving around him like everything was still in place.
Her foot found his under the table. Stayed there.
Outside, someone was mowing their lawn too early for the year.
A dog barked at nothing.
Somewhere a church bell rang once, then stopped.
Later, washing up.
Sleeves rolled. Warm water running.
His wife beside him, drying.
“Something’ll turn up,” she said.
Not looking at him.
He nodded.
“Yeah.”
That evening, the house settled.
Wrappers in a pile.
The smell of lamb still hanging about.
Television on, not really watched.
One of the kids half-asleep against him.
He looked around.
At the small mess of it. The ordinary perfection of it.
Forty nights.
Gone in an hour.
And yet—
here he was.
Still sat there.
Still part of it.
Not everything comes back.

But some things do.
Enough, sometimes,
to get up,
come downstairs,
and stay.

"Yeah"

Just enough to take the edge off.

Just enough to feel normal again.
By day three
you stop missing the high
and start missing the relief.
You would trade pride,
dignity,
months of progress
for five quiet minutes without the pain.
Clinically speaking,
this is expected.
The body does not like losing
what it built itself around.
Day three is when you realize
it was never just a habit.
It was a dependency.
And I am not talking about drugs.

His eyes do not reflect light.
They swallow it.
It is almost all pupil—
a glazed, rusty silver
where the whites should be.
A sudden aging of the hands.
Skin shriveled as if boiled, then cooled—

veins caught beneath it
like orange cobwebs around the bones,
textured like English oak in autumn.
From holding on
to something that would not hold back.
Lips that barely part when he speaks,
raw-looking,
as though they've worn thin from speaking
when no one answered.
Emptiness should be invisible,
but you can see it in him—
like a sad colour.
His emptiness doesn't look
like something taken away.
More like a grey coldness
that was poured into him.

Let's go back to before I said I love you,
before three words carried all the weight.
Let's go back to before you said you loved me.
It's easy, like a Monday morning after an office party.
Let's pretend it never happened.
Let's go back to taking turns buying the coffee
and telling each other what we did and didn't do over the weekend.
Back before we knew what we were risking.

Before we named it.
Before it could break.

He walks away a little slower these days.
His head hangs a little lower,
like there’s something on his mind.
There is an astringent torsion in his eyes,
as if his thoughts are the kind
that leave a man close to tears.
He never looks in a hurry —
he looks like he’s slowing down to stop.
I see him carrying flowers.
I wonder if they are to make her stay
or because she has already left.
I want to ask him,
but I’m afraid I’ll have nothing useful to say,
whatever he might answer.
Maybe it’s nothing.
Maybe he’s happy and they are romantic,
and it’s me who’s inventing the sadness.
Maybe we tell ourselves that
because it’s easier than asking.

Dark hair.
White snow.
Blue sky.
Green pine.
Red car.
Every colour is heightened by its opposite.
And in the center of it—
human warmth
fitting calmly inside winter's brightness,
holding contrast without being consumed by it.
Her hair holds the light differently than the sky does.
The sky is open—wide, almost innocent in its blue—
but she gathers that brightness into shadow,
drinks it in,
turns it into depth.
The wind lifts a few strands
and suddenly the moment feels temporary—
as if she might just as soon turn away.
The sky is almost too blue to be real—
a clean winter blue that feels sharp enough to draw a line.
Snow stretches pale and bright behind her,
but it's her dark hair that anchors the whole frame.
It falls straight and deliberate,
a deep line of shadow
cut against the brilliance above.
The sun stands just behind her crown,

spilling gold through the strands,
turning the edges copper for a moment
before they return to ink.
There's a softness in her smile
that defies the cold around her.
The air looks brittle.
The light is hard.
But her expression is warm—
teeth bright,
eyes narrowed slightly against the glare,
her lips catching the light
like punctuation
at the end of winter's sentence.

Her hand got caught behind the fridge
after she overreached
for a heart-shaped strawberry
that had fallen
and rolled beneath.
She waited for hours.
Nobody came.
She screamed
and shouted
until her throat burned raw.

Nobody came.
These days she is more careful.
She keeps her knife extra sharp—
it's easier this way
to cut free
when something holds her.
Now that she has only one hand
and struggles
to balance
heart-shaped things.

Empty Nest
Saturday morning silence
interrupted only
by the bubbling filter
of a child's goldfish tank
and dust settling.
A quiet emptiness
that sounds like
how sinking must sound.
The deafening clink
of a spoon stirring tea
in a happy birthday mug.
My fluffy socks echo as I pad
between rooms

trying to locate
the end point of silence.
In the centre
of a stiff settee,
flanked by cushions
posed at deliberate
forty-degree angles,
I sit and wonder
where
all the years went.

There is something about your dark hair
against a light blue sky
that sharpens the brevity of it.
There is something about your outstretched hand
and the emptiness between us
that intensifies the urgency of it.
It's witnessed in the brief blinking moments
and the fleeting intensity of your eyes
that makes me ache.
It's found somewhere between the stutter and the euphony
of what I want to say to you—
that I want to get lost inside you.

One day I’ll turn up on your swept clean doorstep —
a picturesque, curated home.
You won’t recognize me
through the tired eyes of your choices.
I won’t recognize
what’s left of you.
Your practiced domestic bliss.
Paintings on the wall
that make us both cringe,
if you’re honest.
You’ll tell me you’re happy.
You won’t convince me you’re whole.
I’ll nod.
Walk away —
no less guilty,
no more free,
just certain
we chose what we could live with

So here we are —
an eclipse.
That poetic moon we shared

snuffing the light we kindled.
Your hand over my mouth.
My hand over your eyes.
Blind and dumb.
The last time we touch
is the first time
we truly feel each other.

He smiled
while watering plants in the rain.
The scraping of his pertex sleeves,
the rhythmic drumming of raindrops on his hood —
it sounded like jazz,
but neither of us danced.
I asked why he was watering plants
in the rain.
He said
because he was told to.
It must be
what drowning feels like.

A brand-new padlock
on a rusted chain

holding two sagging wooden gates together.
The churchyard is closed today.
I will have to find another god
until my god becomes available again.
I was ready to confess.
Now I will have to take
the long way home.

We cut ourselves from one sheet
so no one could say
who began.
Blue-eyed.
Red-mouthed.
Smiling because that is what
flat bodies do.
We held hands
before we knew
what the wood was for.
Behind us,
three shadows
stand upright
like unfinished sentences.
No one told us
how splinters travel

through paper.
No one told us
love can be perforated
along a dotted line.
One of us already knows.
You can see it
in the mouth that bends
downward.
One of us still believes
the heart drawn in red
is protection.
We hang together
because we were folded together.
Because separation
is an act of tearing.
The charcoal darkens.
The drawing pin stigmata bleed
And still
our thin white wrists
refuse
to let go.

Mrs Sheehan was the first adult I didn’t dislike.
She wore a beige diamond-stitch body warmer
and kept her hands in her pockets,

yet somehow could gesture instructions,
wave us onto the school bus
without ever taking them out—
because we paid attention.
I always thought that Phyll, as we called her
once we’d grown familiar,
was the kind of woman who had
a floral tablecloth on the dinning room table
and a husband and children
she loved very much.
We never had tablecloths in our house.
Phyll ushered us on and off that bus
for four years,
and in those thirty-minute journeys
not one of us misbehaved.
No one behaved in our house.
I can’t remember if I ever said thank you
when I moved schools.
Maybe because it’s difficult
for an eight-year-old boy
to explain what makes a person special—
or how I knew
her hands would always be warm,
regardless of those pockets.

Her body had a tog value of 18.
Winter-rated.
Machine washable at thirty.
Her eyes were measured in lumens—
high output,
energy efficient,
guaranteed for 50,000 hours
or until disappointment.
Her waist came with a twelve-month warranty.
Her smile was A/B tested.
Five stars in symmetry.
Four and a half in approachability.
She moved in limited editions.
Restocked every season.
Trending in three countries.
Breathable fabric.
Ethically sourced.
Low-maintenance desire.
Her laugh had a decibel limit.
Her touch was pressure-tested.
Her hips were ISO certified.
Add to cart.
Compare models.
Zoom in.
No one asked
what her grief weighed in kilograms.

No one measured
the wattage of her anger.
No one thought to check
if she had ever wanted
to be sold.

Twenty four hours on a coach
watching Cool Runnings
on a screen I couldn't see from the middle seat,
couldn't understand anyway—
overdubbed in your language.
Twenty four hours on the road
across the most unspectacular scenery of four countries.
In the sonic centre of it all—
snoring, yawning, coughing,
the rhythmic rustle and crunch
of food that won't spoil
in August heat.
Twenty four hours
until I see you again.

in my red cord trousers you'd kept,
your breasts beneath a tight white t-shirt,

framed by the fracture
of a knee-length black cardigan—
its ties blowing sideways
like your unruly brown hair
you blow-dried for the occasion,
the hair you'll sweep back
with your left hand
so I can see it—
the most welcome smile
I had twenty four hours
to think about.

Brightly coloured fruit in a plain wooden bowl,
shot with the lattice shadows of kitchen blinds and February sun.
A lone fly dances against the window pane,
then finds the bowl.
It will not leave—
as if it knows some bruise I've missed,
some softening hidden from the eye,
a sweetness turning inward on itself.
It circles once, then settles near the stem,
where skin gives way at the faintest touch.

Jugendstil and Arts & Crafts everywhere—
the honest weight of wood and stone,
organic patterns, muted pastels.
The reluctant February sun
cast their shadows
across Morris-inspired floral wallpaper,
like puppets sauntering
through cream and purple light.
I leaned against the bare stone chimney stack,
arms stretched along the exposed beams
in my best approximation of a saviour—
half reverent, half ridiculous.
Then she walked past me.
No — glided.
A picture-book red crochet beret,
its weave loose enough
to confess the shine of her chestnut hair—
strands slipping down her cheek.
She pursed her lips
and blew them gently aside,
and in my foolish heart
it felt as though she had blown
a quiet kiss in my direction.
I stepped aside,
as one does
when something rare

passes close enough
to alter the light.

What bothers me most
is that in an easier fate, an ideal world,
I would simply board a plane
and cross oceans as if they were minor inconveniences.
I would instruct you to be at a coffee shop
at 10:30 on a Tuesday.
Not Saturday. Not some romantic hour.
Tuesday. 10:30.
Ordinary enough to be true.
I would tell you to order two coffees.
His and hers.
And take a photograph of them side by side.
Proof.
Not for the world.
Just for me.
Just to see if you did it.
Just to see if you meant it.
If you felt the same quiet pull—
that morphic resonance
I'd pretend was theory instead of hope.
That's how I'd get you there.

And then, while you were framing the cups as provenance,
I would walk up behind you.
You wouldn't hear me.
I would bend down,
slip my arms around you,
I'd breath you in like oxygen,
feel the startled breath leave your body.
You would turn.
You would be so surprised.
Maybe you would cry—
though you insist you don't that.
I would kiss your cheek and taste the salt of it,
the mineral of you,
claim it gently.
We would hold each other
for an indecently long time.
Not speaking.
Not performing.
Just existing in it.
And I would say something profoundly romantic,
worth crossing oceans for.
But I won't write those words here.
I'll save them
for a Tuesday morning
at 10:30
when the coffee is still warm

and neither of us has to pretend anymore.

During a family walk
through a commercial lavender field,
the bee sting blooms—
a red swelling.
It persists.
No amount of
kissing it better
or
let’s get you a lolly
makes it hurt
any less.
The child,
neither distracted
nor compensated
by the gift shop’s lavender
infused sweets and drinks,
served by reluctant teenagers
who would rather be
anywhere else
on a Saturday.

Let's squander this green-leaf, blue-sky enthusiasm
and climb the tree.
Let's fall —
catching our forearms on jutting branches,
tearing skin,
ricocheting off thicker limbs,
hitting the ground hard enough
to knock the wind from our lungs,
and do it again and again.
Trying not to cry.
Six hours in A&E.
A chubby nurse sculpting a six-week sentence
around a wrist
while she dreams distractedly
of holidays,
babies,
and someone who stays.
Climbing again, carefully —
pulling the leafy branches aside
to make it easier for you
with your one good arm.
And not falling.

The postman is struggling today.
All that love to deliver.
A modern-day cupid—
sticky out pot belly, chubby legs in cargo shorts,
a fluorescent orange vinyl sack
packed with clichés and rhyming couplets.
Handwritten red envelopes amidst the brown bills
and government correspondence
look like maple leaves on an autumn pathway,
leaf-strewn Parisian boulevard—
lovers holding hands, stealing kisses,
an onion seller cycling past
in beret and Breton stripes.
Inside the sack:
Perfumed stationery sealed with a lipstick kiss.
Hearts dotted over every i like obedient balloons.
Pressed rose petals leaving faint bruises of red dust.
"Yours forever"
Polaroids of foreheads touching at golden hour.
Promises folded into origami swans.
Mixtapes titled Our Song in glitter pen.
Locks of hair tucked inside like medieval relics.
Silver key charms—you hold the key to my heart.
Hotel matchbooks from the night we first met.
Cinema ticket stubs from rainy Tuesday romances.
Maps with red X's drawn over where it all began.
Necklaces with half a heart waiting for their missing twin.

Coffee rings like halos around confessions.
Rain declared romantic instead of inconvenient and ruinous to the roads.
Sunsets applauded as though arranged by fate.
Destiny invoked like a delivery confirmation.
All of it crammed into his orange sack,
straining at the seams.
He lugs it up stairwells that smell of boiled cabbage,
through gates that shriek on rusted hinges,
across pavements slick with ordinary afternoon.
By dusk his back aches
like an old love story told too many times.
He empties the last envelope into the last slot.
The sack hangs slack now—
just brown bills and silence.
At home
the kitchen light looks faintly orange through the window.
Sara stands at the sink,
hands in grey dishwater,
scraping dried sauce from a plate.
He sets one final card on the table—
his handwriting,
careful as a pressed rose.
Her name on the front.
He rubs the ache from his back
while she dries her hands
on a tea towel patterned with fading hearts.

And for a moment—
in the dull domestic steam—
foreheads touch.
No maple leaves.
No Paris snow.
Just this,
and it's beautiful.

Getting fucked up.
Fighting.
Fumbling.
Being loud and obnoxious.
Throwing up.
Falling instantly in love with girls I French-kissed
beneath disorienting yellow streetlights
outside small-town nightclubs.
Too cool to take their number—
or theatrically tearing it up
in front of an impressionable designated driver.
Bump-starting a fifteen-year-old Honda CG250
I'd swapped for a midnight blue, shiny Jackson guitar
that never suited me anyway,
pushing it a little further down the road
so it wouldn't wake the neighbours

with the young baby.
Listening to "Nightswimming" and "Everybody Hurts"
through earphones beneath a crash helmet
I'd traded a leather jacket for—
with a friend who valued it enough to cover in stickers
I mostly peeled away,
leaving white patches like snowflakes
or cataracts.
Not sure if the rain streaking down the visor
was rain at all,
or tears—
or if it was the weather which
made me feel
so utterly cold and alone.

Left my lungs beneath your duvet
where we were breathless.
Left my eyes on your doorstep
where I told you to look into them
and say it.
Left my mind in the week you went away
and I went out of it.
Left my heart where you broke it—
when it slowly dawned on me,

you weren't coming back.

She lay on her stomach
reading through sunglasses—
the page a dim aquarium of words.
Her sandals rested in a straight, obedient line
at the burnt-orange fringe of the blanket.
The soles of her feet were filthy.
Pivoting on her elbows,
chestnut hair slipped down the long arc of her back,
hemming at the quiet rise of her hips
where red paisley cotton
had ridden up a few centimetres,
her ankles crossed behind her.
I stood behind her, wordless,
waiting for my shadow
to cool her shoulder—
a soft announcement.
She turned, beautifully vexed,
swinging her legs around in one clean motion.
Her hand shielded her eyes.
Her teeth caught the sun.
In the dark mirror of her lenses
I saw myself—
thin, uncertain,

distorted by light.
"I thought you weren't coming."
"I like to take my time."
"Good."
She patted the tie-dyed circle beside her
as if she had been saving it
all along.

As the biological clock ticked through career pathways and milestone achievements,
they fostered a hungry little black girl with a cute little tummy.
Together, they all enjoyed lengthy candlelit dinners,
educating her on morality, ethics, and what it means to be liberal,
over expensive bottles of wine
and pared-down singer-songwriter recordings
on haunting pianos,
performed by well-trained voices.
They took a course in braiding and plaiting,
learned geopolitical histories
to add provenance to their anecdotes.
When they had fed her as much as she could swallow,
they traded her in
for a child more war-torn and urgent.

Dry your eyes.
The sea is not your audience.
The flames do not dim
because you wept in public.
The tide does not retreat
for declarations.
You call it conscience.
It is only spectacle.
Flags start wars.
They do not end them.

A nervous arm, tentatively reaching
around her shoulder on the first date —
the quiet relief
when she softens,
leans in.
Her sweet-smelling hair
in the crook of his neck,
her breath, warm,
stirring the soft bum-fluff attempted beard along his cheek.
He steadies his breathing,

careful, deliberate,
so his racing heart
doesn't give him away.
Paying no attention to the film,
he runs through the choreography in his head —
the stupefying ambition
of rehearsed spontaneity.

The womb-like silence of four a.m. darkness.
The fridge-buzzing head of complete insomnia.
By morning, two swans on a tiny, shallow, man-made pond
circle each other over and over
like platitudes.
I watch from a damp park bench
next to an overflowing dust bin
with the word LITTER written in gold leaf.
Children queue at the foot of a flaky red iron ladder
just to slide down the other side
and run around
and queue again.
A little boy stands beside two chatting women,
his wrist in plaster,
signed by classmates,
resigned to the arbitrary six weeks

that was emphatically explained to him.
Later, bluebells and daffodils in the long grass of a cemetery.
A late middle-aged man steps back ceremoniously
from a vase of mid-priced carnations
and, without intention, mutters:
"we die alone."

The way you recall
the height and colour of every single blade of grass,
every daisy, every scorched yellow buttercup,
the day your mum finished with your dad
for sleeping with a woman called Joan
from his work, " that women "
and your mum took you by the hand
down the herringbone brickwork path,
past the lawn,
and told you not to turn around
as you got into your Aunt Jackie’s car
and she drove you over to her place near—
where your mum and she spoke for a long time,
in the beautifully decorated kitchen, with those draws which closed slowly and a carbonated drinks
maker with concentrates of cloudy lemonade and cream soda,

the door closed,
while you were allowed to watch TV for hours
but didn’t feel like it,

and instead sat there
recounting the grass
and the daisies.

The flattery was consensual.
Then he took the skin
she was saving for someone special.
He split the wishbone
and left her holding
the smaller piece.
The red stain on the white sheet—
she folded it carefully,
corner to corner,
until it buried itself.
She placed it in the washing machine herself
before her mum got home
and saw it.
She had seen
enough disappointment
for one day.

They poisoned the well with the bones they buried.
In the blackness of the pail,

no stars.
Everything on her lips taste bitter now.
Soap on a rope for a clean ending,
a lavender noose for an indigo child.

A hard-faced, middle-aged woman
selling flowers at the entrance to the subway,
where the shadow moved like a sundial,
making her invisible at midday,
forcing her to squint when it was time to pack up.
The rasp in her voice sounded like
too many cigarettes
and pleading apologies around Sunday-night kitchen tables—
apologies to the backs of men's heads,
slamming doors.
She asked if they were for someone special.
When she called me darling,
it sounded like she meant it.
Her hand felt warm and unafraid
as she slowly pressed the change into my palm.
As I walked on, I could barely smell the flowers
over the noise of rush hour,
but I noticed they made some people smile
for a second.
It occurred to me

that probably
nobody ever buys her flowers.

For too long
I stayed in winter’s solace,
numb,
unable to find her.
Lost in the blindness of my shadow upon the shadows .
In spring
she came to me twice:
once in sleep,
and again in the drifting dreams of day,
where thawing warmth distracted me.
She lay in the grass,
sweet-smelling, alive.
Her hair spread around her head
like the sun I used to draw in childhood innocence,
all those reaching rays.
It felt like summer
moving through me,
the seasons of my soul
finally changing.

Sat quietly next to her,
twirling a strand of her hair with my index finger
like a honey drizzler,
counting reasons I love her on the remaining nine.
Lying on her side,
her breasts bunch together
like the rocks people balance
on mountaintops and summer beaches.
There is silvery white glitter on her eyelids—
snow falling toward the curling ebony branches of her lashes;
moonlight squeezing through the curtains,
breaking into sharp stars
across her completely relaxed forehead.
There is a daring moistness to her lips,
the ubiquitous lake in the foreground,
but right now
she is a still life.

For minimum wage
she empties the bins,
pulls scrunched, snotty hand towels
from scalloped sinks,
cleans orange, waxy sebum
from flaking mirrors

fixed with four rusty screws,
and the sticky phlegm of heirs
from the floor beside hissing urinals.
The urine of the children of men of substance
is much like any other urine,
only with a laissez-faire approach to aim,
a salty, uremic breeze
and a top note of boys who wear shoes
you can see your face in.
The purgations of the children of men of substance
are much like any bowel movement—
it all stinks.
Only the ambition smells scournful,
and the indignity of someone cleaning up behind them
is harder to flush away than shit

You were—
are—
my soul mate.
Absolutely no doubt about that.
Nobody before or after
will fill your little boots
the way your skinny ankles
and puny calves do.

No one else's wild hair will tangle in my stubble
as I lie waiting for you to wake.
But I can't bear
to lose even an inch of you.
I wanted all
or nothing.
I can't stand to lose you slowly,
so I made it brutally quick.
Because you were—
are—
my soul mate.

A perfect blue sky after what felt like forever.
The shock of green in a thousand shades.
Remembering warmth on your skin—
and in your heart.
Opening the curtains.
Making a cup of coffee
and finishing it.
In the mirror, caring which way your hair parts,
unpacking the bags under your eyes,
letting them catch the light again.

Listening out for the sound petals make as they fall from a vase
on a beige cork place mat
in the pristine kitchen
of an open-plan flat—
fourth floor,
overlooking a parade of shops
and the car park for a train station as people rush around beneath an imposing anologue clock with
bright orange numbers, which makes a clatter every time a minute passes .

All drowned out by sound of a petal fluttering down and crashing on to a table in an otherwise empty
room.

The potpourri on the bedside cabinet
has lost its smell,
the colours fading
to an indistinguishable blur.
She sleeps on the left side of the bed,
the mattress beginning to list slightly.
If she balanced a memory there
it would probably slip away,
like the rest of them.
She has a wardrobe full of clothes
and no occasion to wear them.
She can’t bear to give them up—
her skin is too thin now,
and she is always cold,

even if the sun insists on shining.

Keeping his hands warm in pockets loaded with house keys,
attached to a yellow rubber smiley face his daughter bought him
for Father’s Day with the money he gave her.
Hood up, ducking his chin into his coat, slowly rolling his head
from side to side to make an amniotic calm,
his stubble stumbling over the chunky plastic zip.
She wears gloves that match her hat,
but not quite the incongruous, pretty colours
of the oversized scarf that could be a blanket.
Her fair skin suffers a flushed redness when it’s cold,
something distraught about it—
so he thinks twice before saying good morning,
and instead pretends to watch two pigeons eating
what he imagines are the remains of a takeaway
a young couple discarded, half-eaten,
in the haste to get a taxi, go home,
and make love.

but it suits the rambunctiousness of the rubbish god they follow around.

simple hand gestures—stop, go—
for the driver to obey.
Either way, it adds value.
It’s good they announce their presence.
The momentary grief of two weeks’ existence,
handed over to a custodian of smelly history
in baggy yellow trousers
and orange volcanised rubber gloves.
Birthday cards left on the shelf
just long enough
not to seem ungrateful or unimportant.
An empty green  bottle of organic gin
that ameliorated a particularly shitty day at work,
the subsequent comfort consumption
of a family-sized bag of crisps,
and the box of chocolates
that had sat on the top shelf since Christmas—
all in the bin, all recyclable,
all memories.
As the dust cart drives down the street
to turn around the roundabout
with a walnut tree in the centre,
and several cars that failed to vie for position
in the limited curbside parking, now making deep tracks on the grass as it never stops raining,
a man stands on the kidney-shaped patio driveway
of his bungalow conversion, wearing a white towelling dressing gown,
as a piece of paper flutters from the back of the truck
and lands on his begonia bush like a butterfly.

reads how someone in one of the other houses
had written:
I love you more than anyone in the world.

having written those exact words
to both his current and ex-wife,
before folding the paper
and walking out to collect his bin,
now empty,
at a jaunty angle to the curb.

the shadows complex.

except her slow breath.

She lived in a thatched cottage about three miles from a beach—
too tidal to paddle in, but stunning
in both summer and winter alike.
She made tea with a ceramic red kettle

If you are out of harmony on December 31,
you will still be out of harmony on January 1st.
If you are at peace now, the year has already renewed itself.
The year does not turn so much as it flows.

Midnight is not a hinge; it’s another bend in the river.
Making vows to become someone else tomorrow
misunderstands the life.
There is something quietly instructive about the disorientation of the holidays,
those days when you lose track of time,
when it’s unclear what day it is,
when meals blur
and ordinary schedules dissolve.
That loss of temporal grip can be a revolution.
It reveals how artificial our usual urgency is.
Without deadlines and clocks pressing in,
life doesn’t collapse;
it softens.
You still wake, eat, walk, speak, feel.
Nothing essential is lost when dates slip away.
Time is not experienced as units,
but as texture.
Not everything meaningful needs to be counted.
Less resolution, more release.
Less striving to improve, more attention to align.
The best way to enter the new year
would be quietly,
not trying to force change,
but making space for it.
Every moment is already a beginning,
and every moment already an ending.

The suffering comes from clinging to the idea
that this moment is special, salvific, decisive.
You will wake up tomorrow with the same mind.
Liberation does not occur by calendar.
But I wouldn’t mock celebration.
I understand ritual as skillful means.
If New Year’s Eve helps you pause, reflect, soften, then good.
If it fuels craving, regret, or self-punishment,
let it go.
“Resolution” should not be to become better,
but to see more clearly.
To notice:
what you grasp
what you resist
what repeats itself quietly
Freedom begins there, not at midnight.
Did you act with integrity this year?
Did you honor your obligations?
Did you cultivate character in small, daily ways?
No grand transformation required.
Just steadiness.
A moral life is built through repetition, ritual, and care,
not dramatic resets.
The new year is a reminder to return to the work, not escape it.
We should respect celebration, family gatherings, remembrance,
but warn against empty promises.

The point is not who you announce you will become,
but how you behave when no one is counting.
Stop forcing it.
Stop clinging to it.
Attend to it carefully.
Meaning doesn’t arrive through achievement,
or declarations,
or systemic validation.
It arrives in presence.

How some things, when heated, release themselves as smoke and vanish.
He began to build a formula.
Not for explosions, though he could have.
Not for gold.
But for something rarer:
Eudaimonia.
The chemistry of contentment.
He studied what hurts.
What heals.
What burns fast and what burns slow.
He noted ingredients:
A measure of curiosity.
Two measures of kindness, difficult to extract, worth the trouble.
A solvent made of patience.
Gratitude — stable when stirred, volatile when cold.
But the catalyst, he found, was understanding, once added, everything else reacted.
Monday came, and with it, the assembly where each student paraded their holiday triumphs.
Plastic gifts. Screens. Bright spokes catching assembly hall light.
They talked loudly, as if sound itself proved happiness.
Then his name was called.
He walked to the front carrying nothing but a notebook, no bicycle to roll beside him, no console to
rig up and deminstrate..

He began to read.
About how humans chase brightness like moths.
How joy is not purchased but precipitated.
How envy dissolves when exposed to empathy.
How happiness is best grown, not given.
The room changed.
The children quieted because they did not know where to place this kind of power.
A boy with a chemistry set had distilled something they could not unwrap, could not plug in, could
not outshine.

He finished with his conclusion:
> Happiness isn’t gifted,
it is cultivated through virtue,
a practice repeated until conduct shapes character,
and character shapes a life well-lived.
No one laughed any more.
Some shifted in their seats, uneasy, uncertain.
He returned to his place, no louder than he began, but heavier with meaning.
And for the first time that year, he felt full.
Not of presents, but of proof.
He kept the notebook, yellowed now and soft at the edges.
As he grew up, he kept the habit of observing emotions like chemicals.
He became a scientist in the truer sense, not of matter, but of meaning, that matters more .

Once there was a man with three sweet daughters and a gentle wife.
He loved them dearly, though he often forgot to show it.
Life tugged at his sleeve, work, bills, noise, the steady weight of responsibility,
and in the midst of all that motion, he held his love like something that must wait.
One early morning, before the house had stirred,
he laced on his running shoes and slipped out into the dawn.
The streets were soft with light, the world not yet awake enough to be cruel.
And there, beside the path, he noticed a small flower,
white, delicate, with four perfect petals glowing like morning frost.
It was beautiful.
More beautiful, he thought, than anything he’d seen in months.
So he plucked it, cradling it as though it were treasure,
and carried it with him, planning to show his family
how something simple could be precious.

He kept it in hand as he rushed through the day,
checking emails, catching buses, unlocking doors one-handed,
digging through pockets for keys and travel cards one handed,
while pressing the flower tight against his palm
so it would not fall, or fold, or be forgotten.
But life, as life often does, called for him.
Daddy, can you help me find my shoes?
he heard that morning.
Not now, he said, distracted,
and the first petal slipped silently to the floor.
Later, at work, a phone call,
Daddy, can you talk to me about school?
Not now, he repeated,
busy with finishing up so he could rush out for lunch
and another petal loosened.
At lunch, a small voice rang through his phone,
Daddy, will you come to my recital tonight?
He barely heard her past the traffic and chaos of people with a half hour window
and when he brushed aside her hope with a sigh,
a third petal fell.
Then his wife called, soft, tired, concerned.
“You’ve upset the girls,” she said,
“they only wanted a moment of you.”
And instead of listening, instead of hearing the concern beneath her words,
he bristled, sharp with defensiveness.
He clutched the flower tighter in frustration,

as though the problem was not him, but the world around him.
When the call ended, he finally looked.
Only the stem remained, stripped bare.
Every petal gone.
Right there, in the crackling florescent light of his office,
he felt everything he had been missing.
He thought of three small faces waiting for him,
of the woman who shared his life with patience,
and of how love, like flowers, does not survive a closed fist.
He didn’t finish his work.
He didn’t explain.
He simply left.
At the station, he stopped before a flower stall,
breathing in the scent of gentleness, of new beginnings.
He bought four blooms, one for each daughter,
one for his wife , tokens of the hearts he had mishandled.
At home, he knelt before his girls,
apologised softly, honestly,
and placed a flower into each small hand.
Their smiles were fragile at first, then warm.
But when he turned to his wife,
he faltered, he only held three.
“I’m sorry,” he began, ashamed,
“I must have miscounted.”
She touched his cheek.
“It doesn’t matter,” she whispered,

“it’s the thought that reached us. That was the missing thing.”
And as he opened his palm to embrace her,
there it was,
the first flower, whole once more,
four perfect petals shining like forgiveness returned it.
He gathered her close,
and for the first time in a long while,
he held love gently.

They say he was born smiling.
It wasnt gas or reflex, not the sleepy curl of a newborn’s lip,
but a true, open, welcoming smile, as though he had arrived from somewhere filled with light and
warmth

and simply hadn’t yet forgotten it.
He never cried.
Doctors worried at first. Nurses whispered second. Mothers in the waiting room crossed themselves
quietly and said maybe Heaven had accidentally misplaced one of its own.

As he grew, he laughed easily, soft, unforced, like rain on warm stone.
He smiled when he was cold.
He smiled when he was hungry.
He smiled when he fell, scraped his knees, learned the taste of blood.
Not because he did not feel pain, because he knew the cost of pain,
because joy was his mother-tongue, and he had no other language.

Some people loved him instantly.
Some said he was simple. Sweet. Slow.
Others disliked him immediately.
They could not understand a happiness that asked for nothing.
It unnerved them. Unsettled them.
Made them feel examined, measured, and found lacking.
“Wipe that grin off your face,” they told him,
and when he didn't couldn't
they took his smile for sarcasm.
The world does not forgive innocence easily.
So they struck him.
First once, then twice, then again for good measure.
They thought he was mocking them with his teeth,
gleaming like a crescent moon while blood pooled at his lip.
He smiled still, because he meant it.
Happiness was not his mask. It was his substance.
And still they struck him, harder each time,
baffled by the defiance of joy that would not break.
It took too long for someone to understand.
A child, not yet taught suspicion, knelt near him
and placed their palm on his cheek.
“He’s not laughing at you,” the child whispered,
“He’s smiling for you.”
But by then,
his chest rose like a question and fell like an answer.
Once. Twice. No more.

When he died, no one spoke for a long time.
The sky dimmed, not suddenly, not theatrically,
but like a hearth slowly losing warmth as embers lose their color.
The world felt colder, meaner.
Something gentle had been extinguished.
Only then did they understand what they had killed:
A boy who carried joy as easily as others carry breath.
A boy who asked for nothing but to give light.
A boy who, smiling, took their violence quietly
and did not curse them for it.
Some say that was his miracle.
Not that he was born smiling,
but that he never stopped.
If you look carefully, some evenings,
just before the sun drops behind old roofs and tired chimneys,
there is a flash of gold across the horizon,
brief as an exhale, soft as forgiveness.
It is the smile the world learned too late to cherish. That's what a sunset is after all, another day of
opportunities fading.

And every time it darkens,
we remember what we lost,
and what we could have been
if we had learned to love the light

It began on an ordinary Thursday, which disappointed him slightly. He always imagined life-changing
events would arrive with thunder, lightening and tense music, or at least a dramatic drop in barometric
pressure.

But no, just a cloudy Thursday morning when his eyes started doing the thing.
On the bus to work he noticed a woman holding her phone like it was keeping her upright. And
behind her ribs, shining faintly like a faulty brake light, he saw a heart with a crack running right
through it. A hairline fracture.

He blinked. Looked again. Still there.
A man reading a newspaper had a heart patched with what looked like parcel tape. A teenager’s heart
flickered like a dying torch. A conductor walked by with a heart so shattered it looked like a dropped
bauble someone had carefully glued back together.

He sat very still.
Tried to pretend this was fine.
It wasn’t fine.
By lunchtime the office shimmered like an emotional hospital ward. Hearts with dents. Hearts held
together by ribbon. Hearts that sagged like wet cardboard. One woman had a heart he could swear was
trying to roll under the desk to hide.

It got to him. Of course it did. He was only human, after all, despite his new unfortunately
superhuman eyesight.

By Friday he couldn’t sleep.
By Saturday he’d stopped trying.
So on Sunday morning, in an ironmonger shop that smelled of shovels and indoor plants dying
quietly in corners, he bought a pot of red gloss paint. The kind used for front doors and brave
decisions.

That night he crept out with a brush and a backpack and started leaving hearts in places where silent
sadness liked to forget it was seen.
A neat red heart on the metal railing of the train station, just above where people stand to say
goodbye.

A heart on the seat of a pub barstool that had held too many lonely elbows.
A heart on a hospital waiting-room chair, dripping slightly because he didn’t stay to watch it dry.
A heart on a park bench facing the river, the kind of bench people only sit on when they’ve run out of
other options.

He didn’t sign anything.
Didn’t want fame.
He just wanted people to know someone had noticed.
But the hearts multiplied.
And people started talking.
Then filming.
Then posting.
Soon he drifted across the country, painting hearts like breadcrumbs or warning flares. People
followed him the way people followed Forrest Gump when he was just trying to run off lonliness .
They wanted answers. Meaning. Maybe a photograph.

He didn’t stop.
How could he?
Now that he knew how much hurt was walking around pretending not to limp.
Eventually, inevitably, it all led to the Houses of Parliament.
A tall building full of important people with very breakable hearts.
He was halfway up the scaffolding, paint-brush between his teeth like a pirate with a dagger, when the
shouting started.

SWAT teams below.
Laser dots dancing.
A negotiator yelling about consequences, safety, national security, the usual.
And a journalist, brave or foolish, perhaps both, cupped her hands and shouted up to him:
“WHY ARE YOU DOING THIS?”
He looked down at her, at the crowd, at the city pulsing with people who woke each day with their
invisible wounds and still managed to move through the world anyway.

And he shouted back, simply, heartbreakingly:
“WHY ARE YOU NOT DOING THIS?”
For a moment, the whole of Westminster fell quiet, as if even history was holding its breath.
Then a single shot cracked the silence.
Red gloss paint spilled down the stone like a final signature.
And the man with the heart-sight fell, pierced through the very thing he’d been trying to protect in
everyone else.

Some say the sniper killed him.
Others say the fall did.
But the truth, whispered by the people who saw hearts differently after that day, is this:
He died of being right.
And the next morning, before anyone washed the stone clean, someone drew a heart there.
A red one.
Glossy.
Perfect.
Unmistakably his.

Every town thinks it invented Christmas, but there is one place, not found on maps , where the
garlands stay up all year.

Not because people forget, but because they remember.
There, no family stays broken for long. Mothers and sons, brothers who stopped speaking,
grandparents who vanished into silence, they all find themselves standing beneath strings of lights that
never learned how to go dim.

And the lights don’t ask awkward questions, or bring up old wounds. They simply glow, warm as
forgiveness.

The houses here were once separated by fences sharp as arguments, brick walls built out of pride,
roads blocked by the rubble of years where nobody crossed. Wars had been fought in living rooms.
Treaties had been signed in slammed doors.
But then came a December with snow falling soft as mercy. Someone hung a paper star in a window
for no reason except it felt right. Then another. And suddenly the whole town was flooded with small,
stubborn hope.

People walked outside holding cups of steam and courage. No one spoke first, but someone smiled,
and that was enough.

The decorations never came down after that. Not in January, not ever.
Children grow up thinking tinsel is just another form of grass. Elders swear they can hear carols
woven into the wind. Even the stray dogs look festive, wagging their tails like bells.

No one here believes in perfect families. They believe in mended ones. They believe a hug can be a
peace treaty, a shared meal can be a bridge, and a single invitation can rebuild a home.

Sometimes visitors arrive, tired from wars they fought alone. Their hearts packed tight with old
winters. But they stay. They see the way love hangs from rooftops, the ease with which a hand reaches
for another, and they decide, maybe they won’t leave, after all.

In that town, Christmas is not a date. It’s a decision.
And the miracle, the real one, isn’t the feast, the star, the gifts.
It’s that every day, people wake up and choose one another again.

through the mud and fire,

no fireworks,

in the bossom of this unspoken ease,
the moment swells,
a private lake of stillness.
Later, if remembered at all,

it will resemble
a faded photograph,
grainy, plain,
easy to overlook.

it is everything:
the quiet proof
that love does not always announce itself,
it simply settles in,
makes itself at home,

Rejoice!
For the High Street has again become the Coliseum of Conscience.
Observe the dry-wipe placards,
their slogans interchangeable as fast as fashion.
This week Palestine,
last Ukraine,
before that Just Stop Oil,
Extinction Rebellion,
and of course when seasonally appropriate
a Pride parade
or a MeToo march
(led by the same men now drafting NDAs).
The same weekend warriors appear without fail:
grief-tourists in fair-trade sandals,
connoisseurs of righteous despair.
The new breed of “morally invested” in causes
that cost them less than a pint because lately they are counting the pennies .
Once, they scolded the plumber
who asked too much for his labour,
importing a cheaper one from Kraków,

calling any complaint “xenophobia.”
Now, their own livelihoods
are undercut by algorithms in Bangalore and A.I that doesn't need a corner office.

They have discovered a nobler economy:
a barter system of hashtags and hashtags,

Hypocrisy is their uniform:
#BelieveWomen until their favourite actor is accused,
#LoveIsLove until two men kiss outside their estate agent’s window,
#SaveThePlanet until the long-haul flight to Bali beckons.
And still they march,
placards aloft,
the last aristocracy of outrage,
the middle class stripped of wealth
but rich in indignation.

and they sip it like champagne
weekends only,
between brunch and Netflix.

the proud, flag-draped patriots of peeling sheds and satellite dishes,

stapled to rotten timber as if they were talismans
against decline.

This is not love of country.

A surrogate autonomy,
hammered onto garden gates
like rusted padlocks on an empty safe.
They call it heritage,
but it is only habit.
They call it pride,
but it is only nostalgia in rags.
A flag does not erase the bailiff’s knock.
It does not fill the fridge.
It does not repair the factories sold for scrap,
or the jobs dissolved into zero-hour dust.
And yet they cling,
as if polyester bunting could redeem them,
as if shouting at the television
were an act of sovereignty.
Their patriotism is not redemptive.
It is ornamental despair,
a bargain-bin sanctity.
A theatre of grievance staged in cul-de-sacs,
half empty pint glasses,
and sheds wallpapered with tabloid headlines.
If the middle classes are connoisseurs of virtue,
these are hoarders of memory,
clutching at faded flags

the way a drowning man clutches weeds.
Perhaps we should all just fly a white flag,
as basically we are all fucked .

the thousand dawns behind us,

each one proof
that disappearance is not the end

that both are one.
